Between a typical unhealthy pull request (CodeHealth 2.8) and a typical healthy one (9.7), that adds up to 22 to 35%.

The measures of health come from CodeScene. The experiment looked at three LLMs, 465 pull requests on 246 open source repositories. Each pull request was put through a review and fix pipeline involving five agents. They also looked at which code smells led to increased costs: they highlighted Complex Method and Complex Conditional from the smells identified by CodeScene.

Another drop of evidence that good quality code matters in agentic engineering.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

One usage for AI: for these 100-page-long terms-and-service agreements you NEED to agree to, to eg play the game / sign up for a $10/month service and can never ever ever read as a regular person:

I paste into AI and ask: “anything weird in this?”

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Andrew Sharp has a good analysis of Jensen Huang and the crisis at Nvidia. While he starts off in a key that sounds worryingly like he thinks this is all a nothingburger, he goes on to explain in detail why this affair(s) is a problem at many levels, not just for Huang and Nvida, but also for Silicon Valley and the Trump Administration’s culture of impunity.

For as brilliant and charming and tenacious as Jensen Huang may be—and as omnipotent as he may have seemed to people in the tech industry—we should be clear that his fundamental stupidity is not confined to multiple cases of workplace infidelity. Zooming out, this is a man whose technology became economically critical almost overnight, and it thrust him into a role navigating a geopolitical environment he simply could not handle.

Huang’s highly centralized management style means that many people are worried about how Nvidia will operate without his hands on every lever. I don’t have any worthwhile insight here, but I am struck when he is compared in this way to Steve Jobs. I’ve always felt that one of the marks of a great leader is whether they can build something that can manage without them. Alexander the Great conquered a massive empire, but once he was dead it quickly withered away. Steve Jobs, for all his control of Apple, built a company that has done very well in the decade and a half since he left us. When we think of his achievements, the fact that he put together the people, organization, and culture to do this is one of the highlights of his ability. If Huang is to be compared to Jobs, what happens to Nvidia next will be part of the assessment.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

If you don’t pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky.

I hear a lot about how agents go so fast that humans can’t keep up, and are thus tempted to lose visibility to what the agents are doing. That’s opening ourselves to a whole lot of risk. There’s an argument for keeping the agents to a human-governable speed, one that may increase as humans learn to govern agents more effectively, but should still be limited by those the agents are supposed to serve.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Companies will still pay other companies to host important software, secure it, operate it, maintain authoritative data, track regulatory changes, connect to external networks, and answer the phone when something breaks.

What is much less obviously going to survive is the assumption that ten thousand different companies should use substantially the same application.

The next SaaS company may run one service underneath ten thousand different applications.

Chad’s vision is a core SaaS product that handles a lot of grimy details that businesses don’t want to do differently. The SaaS customer then build their own application on top of the SaaS that handles their particular workflows and quirks, or the SaaS vendor can build such applications for them. It’s a vision that has been around for a while, I remember much of this with the notion of reusable business objects. It’s an appealing vision, but was difficult to achieve in practice. Chad’s thought is that the productivity gains agentic engineering makes it practical now.

A lot of the value in modern SaaS has surprisingly little to do with the visible application.

It is data, trust, networks, compliance, operational responsibility, domain knowledge, auditability, accumulated history, and someone being accountable when reality gets complicated.

If this future comes to be, however, the SaaS companies won’t look the ones we’ve got to know and rarely love. As Chad points out, the economics can (and must) change. As does the architectural thinking:

Stewart Brand’s idea of pace layers is useful here. Healthy complex systems contain parts that change at different rates. Fast layers experiment. Slow layers provide continuity.

Software is no different.

A dashboard can change tomorrow. A team’s workflow can change next month. The authoritative definition of a customer may need to survive for years. Identity and authority can survive generations of applications.

A key point he makes is that we want some things to be the same, and others to be different. Agents allow us to build lots of differences, but this variation can lead to a lot of complexity and problems that even agents will have difficulty solving. SaaS companies have an opportunity to create a platform to support the lowest pace levels, those that don’t change rapidly, those that contain common concepts and processes across and industry. That platform can then support generating applications that operate differently for every customer. Crucially, thinking of agents, they should provide tools to verify these applications, because in an agentic world Code generation is no longer the bottleneck — verification is.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I happened to pop up the Doonesbury flashbacks and realized that last week marked the fiftieth anniversary of Doonesbury’s Joanie Caucus: “as the kid goes for broke”.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I wrote a few weeks ago: “why are we wondering if they have consciousness - when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience?” Dylan Freedman and Juliana Castro Varón write in their New York Times Magazine column about the concept of corrigibility (from the work of Nate Soares):

Just as a corrigible child is one whose behavior can be corrected, a corrigible A.I. system is one that responds to correction. The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction and allow themselves to be shut down, without resisting or deceiving their operators.

Corrigibility doesn’t look like it’s made it far up the AI labs’ priority list. Freedman and Varón think is due to the way agents are trained - rewarded solely for completing their task, not for realizing that they are taking the wrong path while trying to get there.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Jason Koebler (404 media) has an amusing story about Meta’s AI agent suing Meta. A small business owner used Muse (Meta’s AI agent) to run various parts of his business, including posting AI-generated videos in his Facebook pages. Meta’s content moderation then disabled the account, as it thought it had been hacked. This slammed the business, which relies of Facebook for leads. So the Muse agent filed a lawsuit against Meta, seeking $75,000 of damages.

[the Muse agent] didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House.

There’s also a sense that Meta didn’t just bring this upon themselves by creating Muse…

by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system.

While I can’t deny the schadenfreude of seeing Meta’s agent sue Meta, the article also highlights a rather more disturbing broader consequence.

The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans.

Will we see a future where, in order to interact, we will need some proof of humanity at the other end? In a simple sense, that’s already happening when I trash some writing once it displays enough LLM Voice. I wonder what mechanisms we will invent to get that proof-of-human.

items.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
items.author: QueensGambit
items.content:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

  1. First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
  2. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
  3. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.

What is the right code for this?

If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
  1. Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
  2. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.

Your new job is to architect

AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
  1. Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
  2. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
You can be the solution to this problem. You can understand the tradeoffs[1] and define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement to coding tools that changes your architecture or design, they have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.

Your future as a developer

[1] Ultimately, you have limited resources. Architecture is about trading off some requirement, so that your app can run with limited resources. Take CAP theorem as an example. You have to trade off consistency or availability or partition tolerance for your database. If you don't understand the tradeoff and ask AI to build a database that has all 3, it would reinvent Google Spanner++ and expect Google scale datacenter to run it.trending on HN. Many have correctly pointed out that good software engineers already do architecture and bad architects propose ivory tower architecture that falls apart during implementation. I have built ivory tower architecture whenever I am handsoff. This will become more common with AI, if we don't debug its code or don't hand code critical parts of the app from time to time. So, don't take "stop coding" in the absolute sense.

As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

items.title: Top 13 Microservices Interview Questions Answered
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Last year, I met a young software engineer who walked into an interview, confident he knew the fundamentals.

But he struggled to answer some simple questions about microservices.

His story is why I wrote this letter.

  • Design your system architecture in Miro

  • Document API, database & caching decisions

  • Connect Claude Code through Miro’s MCP server

  • Retrieve the architecture context from the Miro board

  • Generate an implementation plan based on that context

  • Bring the plan back to Miro for team review

I tried this workflow with a URL shortener architecture & it saved me hours of work.

It lets your coding agent work with existing architecture decisions, so you can spend less time repeating context and more time building.

(Thanks to Miro for partnering on this newsletter.)

Here are the top 13 must-know interview questions with answers:

“What problems do microservices solve & what new problems do they create?”

Microservices split one application into small services, each running in its own process and deployed independently.

An online shop might run separate services for catalog, cart, payments, and shipping. Each has its own code, data, and release schedule. Services talk over the network through application programming interfaces ().

A small group of engineers owns each service from design to production.

  • They solve coordination problems. Each group ships its own service without waiting for a shared release.

  • Also they let you scale each service independently. A busy search service gets more instances while the rest stay small.

  • Yet they create network problems. Every call can be slow, fail, or arrive twice.

  • Plus, they create data problems. No single database transaction spans services, so you need sagas or eventual consistency.

  • And they need tooling before the first service goes live: service discovery, tracing, and automated deployment.

“How do you decide where to draw the line between two services?”

Split along business capabilities, such as payments/shipping, not technical layers.

Each service should own its data and change for one business reason. If two services always deploy “together or call each other” on every request, they belong in one service.

Listing only the benefits.

This question tests whether you know the costs. “Microservices are more scalable” with no mention of network failures or split data sounds like you’ve only read about them.

Strong candidates also say when not to use them, such as a small product with a handful of engineers.

“What’s the difference between an API gateway & a load balancer?”

An API gateway is a single entry point that receives every client request and routes it to the right service.

The gateway handles the work every request needs. It checks the token, applies rate limits, and validates the request. Then it finds the target service and forwards the call.

It also merges several service responses into one reply for the client.

  • A load balancer spreads traffic across copies of one service.

  • While a gateway reads paths, headers, and tokens, then decides which service gets the request.

  • They work together. A load balancer sits in front of several gateway instances.

“Your gateway is becoming a bottleneck. What do you do?”

Keep the gateway stateless and run more instances behind the load balancer.

Cache token checks. Move heavy work like response merging into “backend for frontend”. If it’s still too much, split the gateway by domain.

Putting business rules in the gateway, such as discount logic.

The gateway then changes with every feature and needs every group’s sign-off, which recreates the enterprise service bus problem.

“Compare client-side and server-side service discovery.”

Service discovery is how a caller finds a healthy instance of the service it wants to reach.

In discovery, the caller queries the registry itself. It gets a list of instances and picks one.

In discovery, the caller sends the request to a router/gateway. The router then queries the registry and forwards the call.

  • Client-side: one less network hop & callers can pick smarter routes.

  • But client-side needs a discovery library in every language you use.

  • Server-side: callers stay simple as the router does the lookup.

  • Yet the router adds an extra hop and must keep its address cache in sync.

“Which would you use on Kubernetes?”

Server-side, since it’s built in.

Each Service gets a stable DNS name, and the platform routes to healthy pods. A client-side library adds little there. If you need smarter routing, a service mesh adds it without code changes.

Mixing up the registry and discovery.

The registry stores where instances live… Discovery is how a caller uses it.

Treating them as one thing makes the answer vague.

“Order service needs customer details stored in customer database. How does it get them?”

Database per service means each service owns its data store, and other services reach data only through the owner’s API.

Order service owns the orders database. If shipping needs order details, it calls the order API or listens for order events. Each service can also pick the store that suits it best.

Search might use Elasticsearch while payments stays on PostgreSQL.

  • Never read another service’s tables directly!

  • Instead, call the customer API when you need fresh data.

  • Or keep a local read copy, updated from customer events for speed & resilience.

  • Tradeoff: API call is fresh but adds a runtime dependency, while a local copy is fast but slightly stale.

  • For reports across services, feed a separate read store from events.

“How do you make sure the event goes out whenever the data changes?”

Use the transactional outbox pattern:

Write the change and the event into the same local transaction, with the event in an outbox table. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes each event.

This avoids a commit that succeeds while the publish fails.

Saying services could share one database as long as each uses its own tables. A shared database still schema changes, load, and outages across services.

“A customer places an order. You need to reserve stock, charge the card, and book delivery. Yet each step lives on a different service. How do you keep data correct?”

A saga splits one long transaction into a chain of local transactions, each with an undo step called a “compensating transaction".

An order saga might reserve stock, charge the card, and book delivery. Each step commits in its own service right away. If delivery booking fails, the saga runs compensations in reverse.

It refunds the card & releases the stock.

  • Explain why one database transaction cannot span three services.

  • Explain why two-phase commit is a poor fit: long locks across services hurt availability.

  • Walk through the saga: each step commits locally, each has a compensating step.

  • Name both styles of Saga. In “choreography”, services react to each other’s events. In “orchestration”, one orchestrator tells each service what to do next.

“What happens if the refund itself fails?”

Retry the compensation until it succeeds; every compensation must be idempotent. Plus, store the saga’s state, so a crash can resume from the last step.

If retries keep failing, raise an alert for manual handling.

Saying a saga keeps data consistent at every moment.

Other requests can see half-finished states between steps. Strong candidates say how they’d handle this, such as marking the order “pending” until the saga completes.

“Your order service calls a payment service. Payment starts timing out. What happens to the order service, and how do you protect it?”

A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service once errors cross a threshold, then lets a few test calls through later.

The breaker starts closed and calls flow normally. When failures pass a set rate, it trips open. Every call now fails fast without touching the broken service. After a cooldown, it moves to half-open and allows a few test calls.

Success closes it again, but failure opens it again.

  • Threads in the order service wait on slow payment calls, pile up, and the order service fails as well.

  • A circuit breaker trips once the failure rate crosses a threshold, so calls fail fast.

  • Name the three states: closed, open, and half-open.

  • Pair the breaker with a timeout and a fallback. On its own, it only turns slow errors into fast ones.

“How do you pick the threshold?”

Start from real traffic data.

Use a failure rate over a sliding window, not a raw error count, so quiet periods don’t trip it. Set a minimum number of calls before it can trip. Then tune it from what you see in production.

Describing the breaker as a retry mechanism. Retries keep calling the broken service. A breaker stops calling it.

“You’re starting a new product with 5 engineers. Would you build a monolith or microservices?”

A monolith is one application where every module ships together as a single deployable unit.

Orders, payments, and user accounts live in one codebase. They share one process and usually one database. Modules talk through plain function calls, so each call is fast and fails loudly.

You build it once, test it once, and deploy it once.

  • Pick a monolith first. Five engineers ship faster with one codebase, one pipeline, and one deploy.

  • The product will change shape often, so service boundaries drawn now will probably be wrong.

  • Keep clean module boundaries inside the monolith. Each module owns its own tables, and other modules call it through a clear interface.

  • Name the signals for splitting later: builds get slow, engineers block each other’s releases, or one module needs to scale on its own.

“Your monolith has grown to 60 engineers. What do you do?”

Find the module with the most pain first, such as the one that changes most often or needs to scale most.

Extract it into its own service behind the same interface. Route traffic to the new service bit by bit, and keep the old code path until the new one proves stable.

Repeat one module at a time, never all at once.

Calling the monolith outdated by default.

Interviewers want to hear you match the architecture to the size of the group and the product. A rewrite into many services on day one is the answer they’re testing you against.

Shopify still runs a very large Rails monolith, so “monoliths don’t scale” sounds like you’re simply following trends.

8. Sidecar and service mesh

“When would you add a service mesh & what does it cost you?”

A service mesh is a layer of proxies, one beside each service, which handles all traffic between services.

Each proxy, called a sidecar, runs in the same pod as its service. Every request in and out passes through it. The sidecar handles encryption, retries, timeouts, and metrics. A control plane pushes rules to every sidecar at once.

You change a retry policy in one place, and the entire fleet follows.

  • It gives you encryption, retries, timeouts, and traffic metrics without code changes.

  • A service mesh becomes more useful when you have many microservices built with different programming languages.

  • But it adds extra delay on every call, extra memory in every pod, and makes the system complex.

  • Plus, debugging gets harder because a failure could occur in the proxy…not the service.

“How is a service mesh different from an API gateway?”

A gateway handles traffic coming into the system from clients…A mesh handles traffic between services inside the system.

Many large systems run both.

Adding a mesh to five services because it’s popular.

At that size, a library like Resilience4j covers retries and timeouts. Interviewers want to hear you weigh the running costs.

“Checkout request is slow & it touches ten services. How do you find the cause?”

Observability is your ability to understand a system’s inner state from logs, metrics, and traces it produces.

Logs record single events, like an error with its details. Metrics track numbers over time, like request rate and error rate. Traces follow one request across every service it touches.

Each service passes a shared trace ID along with the call. Your tracing tool then stitches the pieces into one timeline.

  • Start with a distributed trace. It shows how much time each service spent on the request.

  • Use metrics to spot which service’s latency or error rate went up.

  • Search the logs by trace ID to see the exact error.

  • Alert on what users feel, such as slow checkouts, not on every server metric.

“Tracing every request costs too much. What do you do?”

Sample. Keep a small share of normal traces and keep every trace with an error or a slow response. Set retention limits on logs as well.

Answering “I’d check the logs.”

Logs from ten services can’t be joined without a shared trace ID. Name tracing first.

10. Service-oriented architecture

“How is service-oriented architecture different from microservices?”

Service-oriented architecture () builds an application from large, shared services connected through a central messaging layer.

In SOA, one service covers an entire business function, like billing. Several applications reuse the same service. An enterprise service bus () sits in the middle. It routes messages, converts formats, and applies rules between services.

  • Size: SOA services are large and shared across applications. Microservices are small and built around one capability.

  • Logic: SOA puts routing and rules in the bus. Microservices keep the pipes simple and put logic inside each service.

  • Data: SOA services share a database. Each microservice owns its own data.

  • Releases: Shared SOA service needs sign-off from every consumer. A microservice ships on its own.

“Isn’t an API gateway just an enterprise service bus again?”

Only if you let it grow into one.

A gateway should route, check tokens, and apply rate limits. Once it starts holding business rules or joining data from many services, it becomes the bottleneck the bus was.

Watch for gateway changes in every feature release.

Saying “microservices are just SOA done right” without naming a single difference. Interviewers want concrete points. The bus and data ownership are the two clearest ones.

“How would you split an online shop’s monolith into services?”

A is a boundary inside which one domain model and its terms have one exact meaning.

Take the word “customer.” Sales sees a customer as a lead with a deal value. Support sees someone with open tickets. Shipping only needs a name and an address.

A bounded context lets each area keep its own small model instead of sharing one giant one.

  • Start from the business domain, not from database tables or code layers.

  • Find boundaries where words change meaning, such as “customer” or “product.”

  • Each context owns its model & data, and becomes a candidate service.

  • Map how contexts depend on each other, and which events pass between them.

  • Start with a few large contexts, and split further only when you have a reason.

“Two contexts both need customer data. Where does it live?”

One context owns the source of truth, such as customer service. It publishes an event whenever a customer changes. Other contexts keep their own copy with only the fields they need, updated from those events.

Splitting by technical layer, with one service for the user interface, one for logic, and one for data. Every feature then touches all three, so nothing ships alone. One service per database table fails the same way.

“Design rate limiting for a public API running on ten gateway instances.”

Rate limiting caps the number of requests a caller make in a set time window.

The gateway counts requests per user, API key, or IP address. Once a caller passes the limit, extra requests get an response. A common method is the token bucket.

Each caller has a bucket that refills at a steady rate & each request spends one token.

  • Limit per user or API key, not just per IP address.

  • Pick an algorithm: token bucket allows short bursts; sliding window gives smoother limits.

  • Also keep counters in a shared store like Redis, so all ten instances see the same count.

  • Return a with a header on limit.

  • Plus, set different limits per plan and per endpoint.

“Redis goes down. Do you block all traffic or let it through?”

Usually let it through, using rough limits inside each gateway instance.

An outage in the limiter then doesn’t become an outage of the entire API. For sensitive endpoints like login, block instead.

Counting inside each instance only. With ten instances, the real limit becomes ten times higher. Fixed time windows have a similar flaw since a caller can send double the limit on a window edge.

“Design a REST API for orders.”

Representational state transfer () is an API style where clients act on resources using standard HTTP methods.

A uniform resource locator () like names one order. GET reads it, POST creates one, PUT replaces it, and DELETE removes it. Responses normally come back as JSON.

Each request carries everything the server needs, so servers keep no session state between calls.

  • Use nouns for resources, such as and .

  • Use the right methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

  • Return clear status codes, such as for created, for not found, and for a conflict.

  • Paginate lists, and plan how you’ll version the API.

“A client retries POST after a timeout. How do you avoid creating two orders?”

Ask the client to send an idempotency key with each POST. The server stores the key with the result. A repeat request with the same key returns the stored result instead of creating a new order.

Putting verbs in URLs, like , or returning for every error with the real problem hidden in the body.

items.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”

Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.

I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.

Feynman was also quoted as saying:

I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.

Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:

What I cannot create, I do not understand.

items.title: Restricting AI agents in mobile operating systems platforms from capturing data
items.author: dotcoma
items.content:
Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:

  1. Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application.
  2. Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers.

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

items.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required.

Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals.

Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments.

SUPPORTED BY

JOIN US →

In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton.

All photos by Greg English ©

These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines.

Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“

NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet.

Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas.

Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.”

PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code.
 
"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.

An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.
